paragraphs.heading: What a vaccine is
paragraphs.text: A vaccine is a biological preparation that gives the body active acquired immunity against a particular infectious or malignant disease. Giving someone a vaccine is called vaccination. Most vaccines hold an agent that looks like a germ that causes disease. That agent is often a weakened or killed version of the microbe, one of its toxins, or one of the proteins on its surface.

paragraphs.heading: How it trains the body
paragraphs.text: The immune system treats the vaccine agent as foreign, destroys it, and keeps a memory of it. Later, if the real, harmful germ arrives, the body recognises its protein coat and is ready. It first tries to neutralise the germ before it can get inside cells. Then it finds and destroys cells that are already infected, before the germ can multiply into huge numbers.

paragraphs.heading: Preventing and treating
paragraphs.text: Some vaccines are preventive: they head off a future infection, or soften its effects. Others are therapeutic: they are used to fight a disease that is already present, such as cancer. Some vaccines give full sterilizing immunity, which means the infection never takes hold at all.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: Inoculation against smallpox was first recorded in 16th-century China, with hints of it there as early as the 10th century. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu carried the folk practice from Turkey to Britain in 1721. Edward Jenner developed the idea of vaccines and made the first one. The word vaccine comes from his name for cowpox, Variolae vaccinae, meaning smallpox of the cow, which he used in 1798 to describe how cowpox protected against smallpox.

paragraphs.heading: What vaccines have done
paragraphs.text: Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent infectious diseases. Widespread vaccination is largely why smallpox was wiped out worldwide. In the United States in 1958 there were 763,094 measles cases and 552 deaths; after new vaccines arrived, cases fell to fewer than 150 a year. By one estimate, the measles vaccine prevents a million deaths every year.

paragraphs.heading: Protecting the whole group
paragraphs.text: When the great majority of people are vaccinated, an outbreak becomes much harder to start and even harder to spread. This is called herd immunity. Vaccines also help hold back antibiotic resistance. Vaccine programs have sharply cut pneumonia from the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae, and with it they have greatly lowered infections that resist penicillin and other first-line antibiotics.

paragraphs.heading: Limits and partial protection
paragraphs.text: Vaccines do not always work. In an estimated 2 to 10% of people the immune system does not respond well enough, because of things like genetics, age, health or nutrition. Protection is also not instant: adaptive immunity can take one to two weeks to fully build, and a person can still be infected during that time. Even partial or fading protection can still lower the risk for a whole population and make illness less severe.
